layout.description: How do you send a whole sentence in antiquity using only fire? In Book Ten of his Histories, Polybius describes a torch alphabet: five tablets, torches on the left for the tablet, on the right for the letter. Reconstructed from the sources; the shape of the devices is schematic.
layout.companion_text:
Historical technology, plainly explained: follow Frontlore.
Reconstruction after Polybius, Histories X 43–47. Solid lines: described in the source; dashed: reconstructed; hatched: not preserved or uncertain. No device survives, only the text (an inference: what is known is the text and modern reconstructions).

unverified: Date of the invention by Cleoxenus and Democleitus: the Kotsanas Museum gives the 3rd century BC on its overview page and the 2nd century BC on the sub-page; on screen only as 'sources disagree'.
Polybius' life dates: born about 208 (Loeb introduction, WHE) or about 200 BC (WHE timeline), died about 126/125 or 118 BC; hatched on the ruler, only '167 in Rome' is secure.
Date of Aeneas (4th century BC) found only at Kotsanas; not on screen.
Loeb note: the tube did not magnify; one source only, not on screen.
Everyday use: Riepl 1913 and Donaldson 1988 as reported by Moore 2017, n. 40, not read directly; on screen only as 'disputed'.
'No device survives' is an inference: known are the text and modern reconstructions (Kotsanas); marked as an inference.

beats.spoken: How do you send a whole sentence across many miles in antiquity, using only fire?
Simple beacons only report what was agreed beforehand. The water clock of Aeneas also knows only agreed messages. Anything unexpected stays silent.

data.headline: WHAT ALREADY EXISTED
data.cite: Polyb. X 43–45 · Moore 2017, p. 120 · Kotsanas Museum

beats.spoken: Polybius spreads the alphabet over five tablets of five letters each. Torches on the left show the tablet, torches on the right the letter. A sighting device with two tubes helps reading.
Each letter therefore needs two signals. To start, the sender raises two torches, and the receiver answers with two. Only then does the message begin.
An example: tablet two, position five. Two torches on the left, five on the right. The receiver looks it up and writes the letter down.
So, three stages: the beacon, the water clock of Aeneas, and the torch alphabet of Cleoxenus and Democleitus, improved by Polybius.
